Benchmarking against other sparse PCA packages

Source: vignettes/articles/benchmarking.Rmd
benchmarking.Rmd

This vignette gives the full benchmarking protocol and results summarised in the package description. It compares msPCA against seven competing implementations on four real datasets, and documents exactly how each competitor was configured — which matters, because the packages parameterise sparsity in incompatible ways.

Chunks are not evaluated at build time: reproducing the full comparison requires eight additional packages, callr for the benchmarking harness, and a Python installation. The memory measurements additionally require macOS or Linux. The complete scripts live in the package repository under replication/benchmarking/.

Getting the data

All four datasets are obtainable from R without manual downloads or accounts, so the comparison is reproducible end to end:

## mtcars -- base R
X_mtcars     <- as.matrix(datasets::mtcars)
Sigma_mtcars <- cor(X_mtcars)

## Pitprops -- the 13 x 13 correlation matrix of Jeffers (1967), Table 1.
## It is transcribed literally at the top of
## replication/benchmarking/notebook_pitprops.R; source that file to obtain `pitprops`.
Sigma_pitprops <- pitprops
## Methods that require a data matrix instead use pseudo-data drawn from this
## correlation structure (see "How each method was configured" below).
set.seed(42)
X_pitprops <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 500, mu = rep(0, ncol(pitprops)),
                            Sigma = pitprops)

## Breast cancer -- one-off download via PMA, then keep the 500 highest-
## variance genes, following the preprocessing of Witten et al. (2009).
X            <- t(PMA::download_breast_data(
  url = "https://tibshirani.su.domains/PMA/breastdata.rda")$rna)
X_breast     <- X[, order(apply(X, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE)[1:500]]
Sigma_breast <- cor(X_breast)          # n = 89, p = 500

## Riboflavin -- ships with the hdi package
data("riboflavin", package = "hdi")
X_ribo <- as.matrix(riboflavin$x)      # n = 71, p = 4088

Only the breast cancer data touches the network, and PMA::download_breast_data() handles it in a single call. Riboflavin ships inside hdi, mtcars is in base R, and the Pitprops correlation matrix is transcribed in the benchmarking script, so no manual downloads or accounts are needed anywhere.

Methods compared

We compare msPCA against seven competing methods:

Package Reference Language Approach
elasticnet Zou et al. (2006) R elastic-net regularization, LARS-like
PMA Witten et al. (2009) R penalized matrix decomposition
sparsepca Erichson et al. (2020) R variable projection with ℓ1\ell_1 penalty
mixOmics Rohart et al. (2017) R regularized SVD (Shen and Huang 2008)
nsprcomp Sigg (2019) R expectation-maximization (Sigg and Buhmann 2008) + deflation
amanpg Chen et al. (2020) R alternating manifold proximal gradient
sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA Pedregosa et al. (2011) Python dictionary learning

scikit-learn is called from R via the reticulate package (Ushey et al. 2025). Together these cover the main methodological approaches to sparse PCA: elastic-net regularization, penalized matrix decomposition, variable-projection optimization, regularized SVD, deflation, Riemannian proximal gradient, and dictionary learning.

Environment

Experiments were conducted on a MacBook Air with an Apple M2 chip and 24 GB of RAM, with R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24), msPCA v0.5.1, elasticnet v1.3, PMA v1.2.4, sparsepca v0.1.2, mixOmics v6.36.0, nsprcomp v0.5.1.2, amanpg v0.1.0, reticulate v1.40.0, and scikit-learn v1.6.1 (Python 3.11). Full session information is recorded in replication/sessionInfo.txt.

How each method was configured

Comparing sparse PCA methods is complicated because different packages parameterize sparsity differently. Some accept a covariance or correlation matrix, others apply only to the data matrix, and some support both.

  • msPCA — mspca() with both type = "Sigma" and type = "X" on all four datasets. On riboflavin (n≪pn \ll p) the p×pp \times p covariance matrix is rank-deficient, making type = "X" the natural choice; we report both modes to quantify the runtime gain.
  • elasticnet — spca(), which takes a list of cardinality budgets (one per PC) and applies interchangeably to 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} or 𝑿\boldsymbol{X}. We report both input modes on mtcars, Pitprops and breast cancer.
  • PMA — SPC() with orth = TRUE. It takes the covariance matrix and a bound sumabsv on ∑t∥𝒖t∥1\sum_t \|\boldsymbol{u}_t\|_1, which we tune manually per dataset to get per-component sparsity as close as possible to the target.
  • sparsepca — spca() applied to 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}, which only exposes the magnitude of the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty alpha. We tune it per dataset to achieve a total sparsity ∑tkt\sum_t k_t close to the target. This method tends to return PCs with very unequal sparsity levels, the first typically denser than the rest.
  • mixOmics — spca(), which takes the data matrix and the list of sparsity budgets.
  • nsprcomp — two functions, both based on the EM algorithm of Sigg and Buhmann (2008). nsprcomp() computes the leading sparse PC then applies the deflation procedure of Mackey (2008) for subsequent PCs; it takes the data matrix and a list of sparsity levels. nscumcomp() solves for all rr PCs simultaneously, taking a total sparsity budget ∑tkt\sum_t k_t and a penalty parameter gamma on orthogonality violation (default 0).
  • amanpg — spca.amanpg() applied to the correlation matrix (type = 1). It solves a single-component problem with an ℓ1\ell_1 penalty lambda1 and applies sequential deflation; we tune lambda1 per dataset.
  • scikit-learn — sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA() via reticulate. The class computes rr components simultaneously using dictionary learning with an ℓ1\ell_1 penalty alpha on the loadings, applied to the data matrix. We tune alpha per dataset.

For Pitprops only the correlation matrix is available, so we generate pseudo-data via MASS::mvrnorm() with the Pitprops matrix as the population covariance (n=500n = 500) for the methods that require 𝑿\boldsymbol{X}.

For each method we report the actual number of nonzero loadings per PC, the FVE computed on the original correlation matrix, the orthogonality violation, the runtime, and the memory footprint. Hyperparameter tuning is excluded from all reported figures.

How runtime and memory are measured

Every repetition of every method runs in its own fresh R process, driven by replication/benchmarking/bench_utils.R. Isolation is necessary because peak memory is read as a process-level high-water mark: several methods in one session, or even several repetitions of one method, contaminate each other.

Memory is peak resident set size, obtained from getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss. R-level metrics such as gc() or bench::mark(mem_alloc) are deliberately not used: msPCA does its work in RcppEigen buffers and scikit-learn in the embedded CPython heap, neither of which R’s garbage collector observes, so an R-level metric would under-report exactly those two methods while fully charging the pure-R competitors. The Memory column below reports the working set, defined as the size of the matrix handed to the method plus the additional peak RSS the method allocates on top of it. The R interpreter and package-loading floor are excluded, so the column is comparable across methods but is not the absolute footprint of the session. It does include whatever a package allocates on its first call — lazy loading of namespaces, compiled code, S4 method tables — which is on the order of 4 MB.

Each method is repeated five times with a different seed per repetition. Runtime, memory, FVE and the orthogonality violation are all reported as medians over the five.

Runtime and memory additionally carry a bracketed range, shown wherever the spread exceeds 15%, because neither is reproducible to the precision a bare median implies. Wall-clock time varies with machine conditions and with seed-dependent iteration counts. Peak RSS varies with when the garbage collector happens to run: two identical runs of the Pitprops benchmark, at identical seeds and with bit-identical FVE and orthogonality, put nscumcomp’s working set at 72 MB and then at 211 MB.

Read the ranges rather than the medians. For the pure-R methods, even the median of five runs moves by a factor of two between sittings, so their memory figures should be treated as order-of-magnitude. msPCA is the exception — its allocation happens in Eigen rather than on R’s heap, and its figures reproduce to within a few percent across separate sittings.

An earlier version of this benchmark called each method once on a small problem before the measurement, to move first-call loading cost out of the memory column. That was removed. Any allocation before the measurement leaves R’s garbage collector with higher heap growth targets, so the measured run collects less often and peaks higher — inflating precisely those methods that allocate on R’s heap while leaving msPCA and scikit-learn untouched, and so biasing the comparison in msPCA’s favour. Carrying the ~4 MB of loading cost in every row is the lesser distortion.

# Representative call pattern; see replication/benchmarking/ for the full scripts.
set.seed(42)
res <- mspca(Sigma, r = 3, ks = rep(4, 3), verbose = FALSE)

fraction_variance_explained(Sigma, res$x_best)
feasibility_violation_off(Sigma, res$x_best, 0)
res$runtime

Tuning: PMA uses sumabsv = 1.69; sparsepca uses alpha = 0.004; amanpg uses lambda1 = c(10, 3, 0.01); scikit-learn uses alpha = 3.2.

Stability across seeds: only nscumcomp varies, with FVE ranging over 0.753–0.823 and the orthogonality violation reaching 0.289 in the worst run. Every other method, msPCA included, returns the same solution at every seed.

At p=11p = 11 the numerical working set of every method is a few kilobytes, so the memory column here measures fixed overheads rather than algorithmic cost. Most methods sit at or below 0.6 MB, as expected. elasticnet, sparsepca and nscumcomp do not: they carry a floor of 16–24 MB that is already present at this size. A single-repetition check confirmed the floor is genuine allocation, not first-call loading, which accounts for only about 4 MB of it.

Pitprops

The Pitprops dataset (Jeffers 1967) (p=13p = 13 physical measurements on n=180n = 180 timber specimens) is a classic sparse PCA benchmark (e.g. Zou et al. 2006). We extract r=6r = 6 sparse PCs targeting k=4k = 4 nonzero loadings per component, as in Zou et al. (2006).

msPCA::mspca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.794 9.4e-05 4.121 0.9 [0.4, 2.0]
elasticnet::spca (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.792 0.241 0.071 21 [21, 26]
elasticnet::spca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.790 0.322 0.162 83 [70, 114]
PMA::SPC (4,4,4,7,6,4) 0.660 0.857 0.014 7.7 [6.7, 9.5]
sparsepca::spca (8,4,3,1,3,5) 0.762 0.376 0.026 18 [16, 20]
mixOmics::spca (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.788 0.215 0.010 2.2 [0.6, 12.6]
nsprcomp::nsprcomp (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.816 0.563 0.027 [0.025, 0.031] 34 [32, 40]
nsprcomp::nscumcomp (5,4,2,6,4,3) 0.845 1.874 0.374 [0.256, 0.916] 148 [73, 187]
amanpg::spca.amanpg (8,6,9,2,3,5) 0.760 1.763 0.011 3.8 [3.7, 5.6]
sklearn...SparsePCA (7,3,4,2,4,4) 0.895 0.733 0.049 0.1 [0.1, 0.3]
PCA (dense) (13,…,13) 0.877 < 1e-15 < 0.001 0.4 [0.4, 0.7]

Tuning: PMA uses sumabsv = 1.727; sparsepca uses alpha = 0.004; nscumcomp uses the default gamma = 0; amanpg uses lambda1 = c(1, 1, 5, 0.4, 0.4, 0); scikit-learn uses alpha = 3.1.

Stability across seeds: msPCA (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) ranges over 0.786–0.822 in FVE and msPCA (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) over 0.784–0.801, in both cases holding the orthogonality violation below 1e-04 at every seed. nsprcomp ranges over 0.813–0.833 with a worst-case violation of 1.105, and nscumcomp over 0.750–0.905 with a worst case of 2.704. This is the one dataset where msPCA is visibly stochastic, an artefact of the random restarts in the truncated power method; what does not vary is feasibility.

This is also the dataset where the feasibility differences are starkest: competitors return orthogonality violations in the 0.2–1.9 range, against 9.7e-05 for msPCA. With p=13p = 13 and a total budget of 24 nonzeros, trivially orthogonal disjoint-support solutions do not exist, so methods that rely on deflation have nothing to fall back on. Note also that nscumcomp reports the highest FVE of any sparse method here (0.845), but does so while violating orthogonality by 1.9 — the two numbers have to be read together.

Pitprops is the one case where type = "X" is the wrong choice: with n=500n = 500 pseudo-observations and p=13p = 13, the data matrix is larger than the correlation matrix, and the O(np)O(np) matrix-free product is more expensive than the O(p2)O(p^2) dense one. Runtime is roughly six times worse than the type = "Sigma" path, though at this scale the memory difference is below what the measurement can resolve. The interface is a win when n≪pn \ll p, not universally.

Tuning: PMA uses sumabsv = 2.92; sparsepca uses alpha = 0.004 but returns unequal sparsity levels; nscumcomp receives a total budget of k=60k = 60 and distributes it unevenly; amanpg uses lambda1 = c(8.5, 2.5, 1.5); scikit-learn uses alpha = 11.25.

Stability across seeds: msPCA ranges over 0.088–0.095 in FVE in both input modes, with the orthogonality violation at or below 9.8e-05 at every seed. nsprcomp ranges over 0.070–0.084 and nscumcomp over 0.078–0.083, the latter reaching a violation of 0.047 in its worst run.

With p=500p = 500 and only 60 nonzeros in total, disjoint supports are easy to find, so most methods are trivially orthogonal here.

This is the smallest dataset at which the memory column measures the algorithms rather than fixed overheads, and msPCA is the lightest sparse method on it by a wide margin: 6.6 MB on the correlation matrix and 3.2 MB on the data matrix, against 270 MB for elasticnet in Gram mode, 121 MB on the data matrix, 132 MB for sparsepca and 51–58 MB for nsprcomp, nscumcomp and amanpg. Only sklearn, at 1.3 MB, is lighter, and it does its allocation outside R entirely. The type = "X" saving is modest here because 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} is only about 2 MB at p=500p = 500; riboflavin is where it becomes decisive.

Riboflavin

The riboflavin (vitamin B2) production dataset (Bühlmann et al. 2014) comprises log-transformed expression levels of p=4,088p = 4{,}088 genes in n=71n = 71 samples of Bacillus subtilis. This is a challenging p≫np \gg n benchmark: the empirical correlation matrix is rank-deficient (rank ≤70\leq 70). We set r=2r = 2 and target k=20k = 20 nonzero loadings per component. To avoid time-consuming parameter tuning, we consider only methods that accept exact cardinality budgets.

Method (k1,k2)(k_1, k_2) FVE Orth. violation Runtime (s) Memory (MB)
msPCA::mspca (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) (20,20) 0.008 < 1e-15 56.700 [46.418, 94.431] 640
msPCA::mspca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (20,20) 0.008 < 1e-15 1.793 [0.852, 2.484] 44
elasticnet::spca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (20,20) 0.004 < 1e-15 6.732 311 [309, 599]
mixOmics::spca (20,20) 0.006 < 1e-15 0.338 24 [24, 58]
nsprcomp::nsprcomp (20,20) 0.009 < 1e-15 0.355 [0.267, 0.377] 54
PCA (dense) (4088,4088) 0.478 < 1e-15 0.047 39

msPCA is run with maxIter = 100 here; all methods other than msPCA (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) use the data matrix directly. Only msPCA varies at all across seeds, and only in the third decimal of FVE (0.008–0.009 in both input modes).

This dataset isolates the benefit of the type = "X" interface. Passing the raw data matrix replaces the O(p2)O(p^2) product 𝚺𝜷\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta} with the O(np)O(np) two-pass product 𝑿⊤(𝑿𝜷)/(n−1)\boldsymbol{X}^\top(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})/(n-1) and never forms the covariance matrix. The measured working set falls from 640 MB to 44 MB, a factor of about 15, at identical FVE and feasibility. The p×pp \times p correlation matrix accounts for 128 MB of that; the remainder is the Eigen copy of it and the dense intermediates the O(p2)O(p^2) path requires. Median runtime falls from 56.7 seconds to 1.8, a factor of about 30 — though both rows vary substantially across seeds (46–94 s and 0.9–2.5 s), so that ratio is worth quoting only to one significant figure.

The memory figures, by contrast, are the most reproducible in the whole benchmark. Both msPCA rows hold to within 1% across the five repetitions, and to within a few percent across entirely separate sittings; elasticnet spans 309–599 MB within a single sitting, and its median moved from 476 MB to 311 MB between two of them. nsprcomp’s median moved from 108 MB to 54 MB over the same interval.

That asymmetry is not incidental. msPCA allocates its working memory in Eigen, where the footprint is determined by the algorithm; the pure-R methods allocate on R’s heap, where the peak depends on when the garbage collector happens to run. The practical consequence is that msPCA‘s memory requirement can be predicted from nn, pp and rr, and the others’ cannot — which is why the competing figures here should be read as order-of-magnitude.

Read together with the Pitprops result, the rule is straightforward: use type = "X" when n≪pn \ll p and type = "Sigma" when p≲np \lesssim n, which is what the relative sizes of 𝑿\boldsymbol{X} and 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} would suggest.

Discussion

Sparsity control. PMA::SPC(), sparsepca::spca(), nsprcomp::nscumcomp(), amanpg::spca.amanpg() and sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA() do not provide satisfactory control over the sparsity of each loading vector, which makes an apples-to-apples comparison difficult. PMA::SPC() and sklearn control only a global ℓ1\ell_1 bound, while sparsepca::spca(), nscumcomp() and amanpg tend to produce unbalanced components with one PC carrying almost all of the budget. It is difficult to calibrate these methods to an exact target number of nonzeros per component. The comparisons below therefore focus on msPCA::mspca(), elasticnet::spca(), mixOmics::spca() and nsprcomp::nsprcomp().

Feasibility. Among the packages considered, msPCA::mspca() is the only method that consistently returns small orthogonality violations on all four datasets, at or below 1e-4 (its default feasibility tolerance). Because every method is now run at several seeds, this is a worst-case statement rather than a single-run one: across all repetitions on all four datasets, the largest violation msPCA returned was 9.9e-05. All other packages can return substantially non-orthogonal components, especially when pp is small relative to the total sparsity budget, so that trivially orthogonal disjoint-support solutions may not exist.

Variance explained. msPCA::mspca() and nsprcomp::nsprcomp() are generally the best-performing methods, followed by mixOmics::spca() and elasticnet::spca(), though the relative ranking of the latter two varies across datasets. msPCA does not appear to sacrifice variance explained in order to achieve feasibility. The one method that outperforms it on FVE while respecting the cardinality budget is nscumcomp on Pitprops, which reaches 0.845 against 0.791 — but with an orthogonality violation of 1.9, and with a spread of 0.750–0.905 across seeds, so the comparison is not like for like.

Reproducibility. Repeating each method under several seeds separates the deterministic implementations (elasticnet, PMA, sparsepca, mixOmics, amanpg, dense PCA) from those that are not. nsprcomp and nscumcomp use random initialisation and can move substantially between runs — nscumcomp’s FVE spans 0.750–0.905 on Pitprops and its orthogonality violation 1.9–2.7. msPCA uses random restarts and is also not bit-reproducible across seeds, but its variation is confined to the objective: the feasibility guarantee holds at every seed on every dataset, the largest violation observed anywhere being 9.9e-05.

Memory. On the two high-dimensional datasets, where the memory column reflects the algorithms rather than fixed overheads, msPCA is the lightest of the sparse methods that respect an exact cardinality budget. On breast cancer it uses 3.2 MB on the data matrix against 121 MB for elasticnet on the same input and 270 MB in Gram mode, with sparsepca at 132 MB and nsprcomp, nscumcomp and amanpg in the 51–58 MB range. On riboflavin it uses 44 MB against 311 MB for elasticnet. The 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}-versus-𝑿\boldsymbol{X} choice matters more than the choice of package: msPCA itself spans 640 MB to 44 MB on riboflavin depending on which interface is used.

msPCA’s memory figures are also markedly more stable, because it allocates in Eigen rather than on R’s heap, where peak footprint depends on garbage-collector timing. Its riboflavin figures reproduce to within a few percent across separate sittings, whereas elasticnet’s median moved from 476 MB to 311 MB and nsprcomp’s from 108 MB to 54 MB between two runs of the identical script. For a user sizing a job, a predictable requirement is worth as much as a small one; the competing figures quoted above should be read as order-of-magnitude.

Scalability. msPCA::mspca() scales to datasets with pp in the thousands in reasonable time, and the type = "X" interface yields substantial runtime and memory gains when n≪pn \ll p — roughly 30x faster and 15x lighter on riboflavin. When n>pn > p, as in the Pitprops pseudo-data, the ordering reverses and type = "Sigma" is preferable.
